# What efficiency can still tell us {#sec-implications}

Standardization makes efficiency comparisons more informative. Public training
data and common resource accounting remove some benign explanations for an
outlier. They do not make the conditional rule require secret training facts:
the construction retains the legitimate implementation and changes its
behavior on a specified subset of inputs. A finite training set containing no
trigger gives $f$ and $g$ identical answers. This does not show that a prescribed,
verifiably executed training algorithm would select $g$.

Nor does the result defeat exact verification. An oracle that checks correctness
on every input rejects $g$; a release rule requiring an exact minimum with zero
tolerance is not refuted by an implementation with $k$ extra gates. The result
addresses nonzero resource tolerance coupled to incomplete behavioral evidence.
At fixed $k$, the relative overhead $k/C_\star(f)$ vanishes as legitimate task
complexity grows, while the conditional error remains total.

Related work establishes stronger or more concrete results along other axes.
ONEFLIP demonstrates triggered behavior after a single stored-weight bit flip
in vision models [@li2025oneflip]. Its modification count is not the storage
cost of a complete hidden policy. Goldwasser et al. construct computationally
undetectable backdoors under cryptographic assumptions, including a white-box
result for particular model families [@goldwasser2024backdoors]. Our transparent
construction makes no such undetectability claim. Its purpose is to expose the
resource-accounting error without requiring either neural experiments or
cryptography.
<!-- ref: research/efficiency-and-alignment/papers/conditional-reuse/related-work/retrieval.md; primary-source support and scope -->

Efficiency can therefore remain one practical warning signal: unexplained
excess capacity is a reason to investigate. Absence of conspicuous excess is
weak reassurance against a short conditional rule. Treating efficiency as an
alignment certificate would require additional assumptions connecting small
implementation cost to the absence of the particular unwanted behaviors at
issue.

# Future work {#sec-future}

A stronger theoretical guarantee would specify a model class, permissible
interventions, and unwanted behavior family, then lower-bound the additional
resources required for every member of that family. Such a bound would have
to charge for reuse of existing features and distinguish passive testing from
targeted inspection. Whether useful bounds survive those choices remains open;
the elementary construction here rules out assurances that omit them.
